Lakshmana's Night Discourse to Guha

Stories from the Ramayana

Lakshmana's Night Discourse to Guha

The first night at Shringverpur — Lakshmana speaks to Guha

In everyday English — Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is one night — and one conversation. On the first night of exile, by the banks of the Ganga, Guha is full of grief — and Lakshmana slowly, gently explains things to him. This is not a story of war; it is a story of a troubled mind finding peace. Where Guha grieves, read slowly; where Lakshmana speaks, read with pauses.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Guha sorrowful, Lakshmana soft and steady.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak. The questions in this book are not easy ones — and their answers are not single ones either.

The whole story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda, dohas 89–93. It is not the story of Valmiki's Ramayana — it is the night as Tulsidas tells it. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya. Warm dark-brown skin, a plain gold crown, barefoot in the forest. On the first night of exile he sleeps on a bed of grass and leaves by the Ganga.

Sita — with Rama in the forest. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a simple muted green-beige saree, no crown.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, beside him at every step. Like Rama, a little lighter in complexion, bow in hand. This night he stands guard — and explains things to Guha.

Guha — chief of the Nishadas, king of Shringverpur. Rama's friend, a man of the banks of the Ganga. This night he sits beside Rama — and his heart is full of grief.

Sumantra — minister of Ayodhya, who has come to see Rama to the forest.

1 · The First Night at Shringverpur · · THE FIRST NIGHT AT SHRINGVERPUR

Rama had left Ayodhya — for exile in the forest. With him were Sita and Lakshmana — and the minister Sumantra, who had brought them in his chariot.

After the first day's journey they reached the banks of the Ganga — Shringverpur. Guha, chief of the Nishadas, lived there. Guha was Rama's friend — he welcomed Rama and gave him bulbs, roots and fruits.

Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Sumantra ate the bulbs, roots and fruits. Then Rama lay down on a bed of grass and leaves — a prince of the royal palace, sleeping on the earth. Sita lay down beside him.

Lakshmana pressed Rama's feet — until Rama fell asleep. Then he said softly to Sumantra — “Go and rest now.” — and himself, bow and arrows ready, sat a little way off in the hero's posture and kept watch.

Guha called his trusted watchmen — and stationed them here and there with great love. Then he himself, quiver fastened to his waist and an arrow fitted to his bow, came and sat beside Lakshmana.

Pause and think — Rama could have slept in a palace — but he sleeps on a bed of grass. Is a king sleeping on grass itself the exile — or is exile something else? And Lakshmana keeps watch — is keeping watch also a kind of service?

2 · Guha's Grief · · GUHA'S GRIEF

The night grew deep. The fire burned low, the Ganga flowed slowly, the stars twinkled above.

Guha looked — his lord, the prince of Ayodhya, sleeping on grass. Seeing this, grief welled up in Guha's heart. The hair on his body bristled with love — and tears flowed from his eyes.

Guha said to Lakshmana — “Lakshmana, what has happened? How beautiful was Ayodhya's palace — its rooftops built of precious gems, the fragrance of flowers, a home full of comfort and joy. And today Rama lies here — on a bed of grass!”

“Kaikeyi has played the axe in felling the tree of the solar race — she has plunged the whole world in sorrow. All of this happened because of her!”

Weeping, Guha went on — “Why did Rama have to come to the forest at all? Who did this? Who is to blame?”

Lakshmana looked at Guha — and said nothing. He knew — when grief wells up, first it must be allowed to flow.

(Read this part softly — Guha is weeping.)

Pause and think — Guha is weeping — and he blames Kaikeyi. When we are in sorrow, do we too blame someone? And does blaming lessen sorrow — or make it grow?

3 · No One Gives Another Joy or Pain · · NO ONE GIVES ANOTHER JOY OR PAIN

Then Lakshmana spoke — in sweet, gentle words — words in which the nectar of wisdom, dispassion and devotion was mixed.

Lakshmana said — “Brother, no one gives another joy or pain. Everyone reaps the fruit of one's own actions.”

Tulsidas wrote Lakshmana's words like this —

“Kahu na kou sukh dukh kar data, nij krit karam bhog sabu bhrata.” — No one gives another joy or pain, brother — everyone reaps the fruit of their own deeds.

Lakshmana explained — “Guha, what has happened did not happen because of one person alone. It is easy to blame Kaikeyi — but the truth is that with everyone, what happens is what their own deeds have made.”

Guha listened in silence. The flames of the fire moved slowly.

Pause and think — Lakshmana says — no one gives another joy or pain. Does this feel true? When someone causes us pain — do they truly give us the pain, or does our own mind make it?

4 · Meeting and Parting, Friend and Foe · · MEETING AND PARTING, FRIEND AND FOE

Lakshmana went on — “Union and separation, pleasurable and painful experiences, what helps and what harms, friend and foe and the one in between — these are all snares of delusion.”

“Birth and death, prosperity and adversity, destiny and time — and all the illusion of the world — these too are delusion.”

Lakshmana said — “Lands, houses, wealth, town and family, heaven and hell — whatever is seen, heard, or thought of with the mind — its root is ignorance. In the highest truth — it is nothing at all.”

Guha asked — “Then is all of this — this home, this town, this family — nothing real at all?”

Lakshmana said — “What changes is not the lasting truth. What is today and will not be tomorrow — that is like a dream.”

Pause and think — Friend and foe — do they stay friend and foe forever? Does a friend ever become a foe — and a foe a friend? And meeting and parting — is parting also a part of life, just as meeting is?

5 · The World Is Like a Dream · · THE WORLD IS LIKE A DREAM

Then Lakshmana said one small thing — a thing anyone could understand.

“Sapne hoi bhikhari nripu, ranku nakpati hoi. Jage labhu na hani kachhu, timi prapanch jiyan joi.” — In a dream a king becomes a pauper, and a pauper becomes the lord of paradise. But on waking, neither gains nor loses anything. Look upon the world in just the same way.

Lakshmana explained — “In a dream, whether you become a king or a pauper — the moment you wake, the dream breaks. Neither the king's kingdom remains, nor the pauper's begging. The world is just like that — while the sleep of delusion lasts, all of this feels real.”

Guha closed his eyes — and thought. In dreams he too had been a king — the chief of Shringverpur. And now — Rama's friend, sitting on the banks of the Ganga.

“Then is this night too — a dream?” — Guha asked softly.

Lakshmana said — “As long as we sleep in delusion, everything is a dream.”

Pause and think — In a dream a king becomes a pauper — and on waking nothing changes. Does this happen in the daytime too — that we take something to be very great, and later it seems to have been nothing at all?

6 · The One Who Stays Awake in the Night of Delusion · · THE ONE WHO STAYS AWAKE IN THE NIGHT OF DELUSION

The night grew deeper still. The fire was low now — only embers glowed. Rama and Sita slept. Sumantra slept. The watchmen were at their posts.

Lakshmana said — “Guha, in this night of delusion everyone is asleep — and asleep, everyone sees dreams of their own.”

Lakshmana said — “In this dark night, only the yogis stay awake — those who seek the highest truth, and remain apart from the world.”

Guha asked — “Then what should people like us do — who are neither yogis nor wise? How do we wake?”

Lakshmana said — “Hold on to Rama's feet, Guha. Devotion to Rama is the way to wake from this night. Whoever holds on to Rama wakes from the sleep of delusion — and then no dream frightens him.”

Guha looked toward Rama — sleeping on his bed of grass. And his heart grew lighter — as if a weight had lifted.

(Pause here — the weight is lifting from Guha's heart.)

Pause and think — Everyone sleeps — only the yogis stay awake. Is waking only about opening one's eyes — or is the waking of the mind something else? And Lakshmana says — hold on to Rama. Can holding on to someone — taking someone's support — also be a way to wake?

7 · Morning Came · · MORNING CAME

The night passed. A soft light spread in the east — the stars went out one by one. The first ray of morning fell on the Ganga.

Guha was calm now. His grief had not gone away — but it had grown lighter. He understood — that Rama had to come to the forest was not one person's fault. And Rama was here beside him — that was enough.

Rama woke. Sita woke. Sumantra woke. All bowed to the Ganga.

Ahead lay the crossing of the Ganga — and Guha had a boat. But that story — is in the book of Kewat.

The story of this night ends here — a grieving heart, a quiet conversation, and a morning.

Pause and think — All night Guha grieved — and in the morning he is calm. Did the night's conversation change him — or did he change his own mind? And when our hearts are heavy — can a conversation also be a medicine?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source — Ramcharitmanas

The whole story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda, dohas 89–93. The meal of roots and fruits, Rama sleeping on a bed of grass, Lakshmana pressing his feet and keeping watch, Guha stationing watchmen and sitting beside Lakshmana, Guha's grief and his blaming of Kaikeyi, and Lakshmana's teaching — all of it is in dohas 89–93.

Guha's Grief

Guha's words that Kaikeyi played the axe in felling the tree of the solar race and plunged the whole world in sorrow — this is the story around dohas 90–91, as Tulsidas tells it.

Lakshmana's Teaching

“No one gives another joy or pain; everyone reaps the fruit of their own deeds” — this is the teaching of doha 91. Union and separation, friend and foe, birth and death, destiny and time, lands, houses, wealth, family, heaven and hell — all delusion, rooted in ignorance — this is the story of dohas 91–92. The dream example is in doha 92. All sleeping in the night of delusion, and the yogis staying awake — this is around doha 93.

There Is No Equivalent in Valmiki

This is worth noting — there is no such discourse by Lakshmana in Valmiki's Guha episode. Valmiki tells of the night at Shringverpur, and later Guha tells Bharata that Lakshmana comforted them — but this teaching about maya, karma and the dream is not there. This discourse belongs to Tulsidas alone. So do not read this book as Valmiki's story.

Shringverpur — the Place

Shringverpur is the place on the banks of the Ganga where Rama spent the first night of exile. Tradition links it with Singraur, near present-day Prayagraj — this is a traditional identification, not something proven by archaeology.

About the Pictures

All the pictures in this book are of the night — on the banks of the Ganga, under the stars, in firelight. There is no daytime picture, because this is a story of the night. In the dream picture, the king and the pauper appear only in the cloud of the dream — not as a real scene.

What Happens Next

In the morning the Ganga had to be crossed — and Guha had sent for a boat. The story of crossing the Ganga is in the book of Kewat.
